intro.summary: Build Target Rush. Click ten targets in twenty seconds. The game tracks your score, shows a timer, handles wins and losses, and lets you restart.
prepare.heading: 1. Set up the project and OpenGL
prepare.body: Create Limen/target-rush. Copy build.hxml and the native files from the first window tutorial, then add opengl.limen from the same build. You need a working driver that supports OpenGL 3.3 or later.
source.heading: 2. Copy the game code
source.body: Save the code as target-rush/Main.hx. The game draws rectangles by limiting where OpenGL clears the framebuffer. This keeps the project in one file, with no textures or shader files.
play.heading: 3. Play a round
play.step.1: In a terminal opened in target-rush, run haxe build.hxml, then hl main.hl or .\hl.exe main.hl with the bundled Windows runtime.
play.step.2: Left-click the green targets. Each hit adds a point and moves the target. The blue bar at the bottom shows the time left.
play.step.3: Try winning, letting the timer run out, and hitting targets after resizing the window. Press <kbd>R</kbd> to start another round or <kbd>Esc</kbd> to quit.
explain.heading: How the game works
explain.step.1: The loop polls for events. On a click, it checks whether the pointer is inside the target and updates the score. The variables score, targetX, targetY, and deadline store the round state.
explain.step.2: Time.now() returns seconds elapsed since SDL's timer started. Subtracting the current time from the deadline gives the time left, regardless of how many frames have rendered.
explain.step.3: Clicks use window coordinates, while OpenGL draws in physical pixels. Positions expressed as fractions from 0 to 1 map between the two, including on high-DPI displays.
explain.step.4: State.scissor restricts the clear to a rectangle. OpenGL's origin is at the bottom, so the target's Y position becomes height - bottom. context.present() displays the finished frame.
extend.heading: Make it your own
extend.body: Change GOAL, ROUND_SECONDS, and TARGET_SIZE. Add a penalty for misses or shrink the target after each hit. For sprites and shaders, continue with the OpenGL guide. To save a high score, see the Paths example.
